blocks.text: INNNEWS - Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI), a global stock market index provider who became an institutional investor reference, on October 15, 2026 announced a consultation for the change in Indonesian classification of Emerging Market to Standalone Market, by highlighting the transparency of stock ownership and coordinated trade allegations. MSCI also maintains freezing Indonesian stock changes in its index, while final decision of reclassification scheduled the slowest end of June 2027.

There's something bigger than the stock price movement in a 30.25% exchange of subterranean PT Resources Tbk (BYAN) shares to P.T Jhonlin Baratama, a company associated with Haji Isam entrepreneur. The issue lies in a meeting between the transaction worth Rp26.1 trillion, the stock of an affiliate company that was deposited to the Manself Bank, and the extreme pressure that hit the Indonesian capital market when MSCI questioned market transparency.

On October 7, 2026, Jhonlin Baratama completed the purchase of approximately 10.08 billion BYAN shares at Rp2.588 per share price, with transaction value around Rp26.09 trillion. The price is well below the BYAN stock price on the regular market. Based on Rp11,200 closing prices on October 6, the discon is at about 76.9%. The price difference between a block deal and a regular market doesn't automatically prove a breach, but a difference of that size deserves a transparent explanation.

The next development makes that question even more relevant. On October 13th, Low Tuck Kwong bought 500,000 BYAN shares at Rp11,200 a share. A day later, he went back to buying 10,000 shares at the same price, with a value of about Rp1.12 trillion. After the second transaction, his ownership went up from about 9.95% to 10.25%. In the openness of information, the purchase is declared to be an investment.

Thus, just a few days after selling most of his ownership through block transactions at Rp2,588 per share, Low returns buy BYAN stock at Rp11,200 per share. The price of repurchase was more than four times the price of previous block transactions. They don't necessarily prove manipulation, because both transactions go on in different context and mechanisms. However, economically, that large difference in prices raises a fair question: what is the basis of price exchange block, how is the structure of the deal, and what information is there for investors to understand the sequence of these transactions?

The next question is about financing. On September 30, 2026, Jhonlin Agro Ramah (JARR) and Gunatama's (PGUN) Predictions were reported to the Self Bank as part of a credit facility for an affiliated company. According to the public report, about 7.99 billion shares of JARR and 5.30 billion shares became collateral. The combined market value was estimated to reach Rp73 trillion based on prices in early October. That number is an estimate of collateral market value, not given credit.

This is where the public matters begin. Does a credit facility guaranteed JARR and PGUN shares have a direct relationship with the BYAN acquisition? Are both transactions part of a interconnected financial strategy? There hasn't been enough public evidence to make sure that the Money Bank credit is used directly to buy BYAN. The Bank of Self states that the facility is meant for the capital and the need for coal and its support sector, with stocks as an additional collateral form. That explanation should be noted, but it doesn't eliminate any questions regarding credit exposure and collateral risk.
When the Stock Assign faces Market Pressure

On Friday, October 16th, 2026, the Indonesian stock market suffered extreme pressure. IHSG plummeted sharp, while PGUN closed down 14.91% to Rp6.850 and JARR down 14.98% to Rp2.270. The drop occurred when investors were looking at MSCI announcements about consulting on possible changes in Indonesian classification from Emerging Market to Standalone Market.

Finally, these events show the risks that are worth testing. If the razed stock prices go down, collateral markets go down. If the drop continues and the debtors face difficulty of paying, the creditors' protection can be weakened. The risks become more complex when collateral stock comes from the same group of businesses and is under pressure simultaneously.

This is what in popular language reminds us of Murphy Az Law: when some risks come together, the system is tested not based on ideal conditions, but it has the ability to deal with bad scenarios. In financial terms, analysis is related to collateral risk, concentration credit, and possible wrong@-@ way risk, which is the state when the risk of creditors increases simultaneously with the demolition of the factor that sustains the value of credit protection.

However, the decline in stock prices does not automatically mean that credit is problematic or bank loss. The Bank of Self states that JARR and PGUN stock are not the only collateral. To know the actual risk, it takes information about credit balance, collateral value recognized after risk adjustments, facility provisions and cash debtors' ability. It's not just collateral markets on paper, it's how much realistic value can be realized when it fails to pay.

Public interests are getting bigger because the Self-Bank is a state-owned bank in the ecosystem of state ownership through Dantara. This status doesn't mean that the state banks shouldn't give credit to private businessmen. Instead as a commercial bank, the Self-Bank should be able to channel productive credit and manage professional risk. The public has the right to question whether careful principles are applied adequate when a credit facility, stock collateral, and corporate transactions are worth tens of trillion rupees appear within a adjacent time span.
BYAN and the Indonesian Modular Market Exam

The BYAN issue is based on the MSCI concerns about the transparency of ownership structures, the alleged coordinated trade behavior, and the need for reforming that can be proven. MSCI does not state that BYAN transactions are the sole cause of proposal for changes in Indonesian classification. Therefore, direct-due relationships should not be assumed. However, this sequence of transactions is relevant as a case study to test the quality of information openness and control of the Indonesian capital market.

A healthy market doesn't prohibit a block deal at a different price from a regular market. A healthy market ensures that the transaction is understandable, reported as per the terms, and is properly monitored. When a shareholder sells a large block at a much different price, then buys back stock at a higher price in a matter of days, investors are entitled to an explanation for the context of the economy and its transaction mechanism.

Similarly, the use of stock as collateral credit is a legitimate practice. However, if collateral concentrations are concentrated on the vulnerable stock experiencing a sharp decline, risk management quality becomes relevant questions. OJK and BEI need to ensure adequate information openness, while the Self-Bank needs to be able to show that credit and collateral assessment follows the prevailing principle of caution.

The term for the BYAN scandal in this article is an opinion frame to test possible management issues, not a verdict that a felony has been committed. It's not just the profit or the loss of one businessman, it's the credibility of the system that merges stock transactions, banking financing, and the interests of public investors.

Indonesia can't build a global class capital market by relying on economic growth or massive market capitalization. A credible market requires information openness, investor protection, and consistent supervision. The BYAN transaction sequence, repurchase of stock by Low Tuck Kwong, the guarantee of JARR and PGN stock, and the price drop on October 16 is worth checking as a series of questions, although the direct link between all of those transactions has yet to be proven.

The most important question is not whether Haji Isam gains a profit or whether the Bank of Self will surely lose. The question is whether the transaction structure, credit and collateral facilities have been designed as well as being watched by considering market pressure scenarios makes sense. If everything is properly managed, transparency will strengthen trust. If there's a weakness, the public has a right to know how regulator and bank management handle it.

The BYAN stock can go up or down. However, the size of the stock market credibility is not a one-day stock price movement. The size is whether investors can trust a system that determines how stock is owned, traded, judged and watched.
Because, when private transactions are worth tens of billions of dollars in cash, transparency is not just a corporate business. He's become a public matter.
By the doctor Hanny semanaga, M.B.A.
